job: Clock spring (steering wheel spiral cable) replacement
unit: per job: the one clock spring (also called spiral cable, cable reel or steering wheel coil) under the steering wheel, fitted. Not included: the driver airbag module, a steering angle sensor where it is a separate part, diagnosis or code scanning, and any steering angle sensor recalibration unless the stated time says it covers it
held_reason: Every class is missing its aftermarket (low) parts price: no retailer page was found that lists a new aftermarket clock spring with fitment for the example vehicle (the pages found either do not say new, do not list fitment, or sell the genuine part). Truck and luxury have no high labor figure. The luxury labor time (1.2 flat rate hours, 'Replace Spiral Cable') may include the serial-number inspection: the sister Toyota letter prints the same 1.2 against 'Inspect and Replace Spiral Cable'. The economy 0.9 M/H is printed on Hyundai's dealer notification for the whole bulletin; in the bulletin's own table it sits on the Sonata row and no separate time could be read on the Elantra row. The midsize and economy high (2 hours) is a signed DIY guide written for the Elantra, not the Santa Fe. Benchmarks: only two independent publishers (the third quotes RepairPal).

finding: New job, so there is no live range to judge. This file is not complete. What is solid: a maker-stated labor time for every class and a dealer list price for every class. What is missing: an aftermarket new price for every class (low parts end is null everywhere) and a high labor figure for the truck and luxury classes. Built totals, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), can therefore only be given at the top end or on list-price parts. Economy 2013 Hyundai Elantra: top end about $484 (list $164.40 + 2.0 hr x $160); labor alone at the low end is about $108 (0.9 hr x $120). Midsize 2008 Hyundai Santa Fe: top end about $762 (list $442.37 + 2.0 hr x $160); labor alone at the low end is about $60 (0.5 hr x $120). Truck 2010 Toyota Tacoma: with the list-price part and the one stated time, about $324-$360 ($216.22 + 0.9 hr); no range can be built. Luxury 2023 Lexus NX 350: with the dearest list-price part and the one stated time, about $593-$641 ($449.09 + 1.2 hr); with the cheapest listed number ($253.78) about $398-$446. These sit below the benchmarks ($500-$1,200 and $627-$731), which is expected when labor is a warranty time. How solid the labor times are: all four low ends are manufacturer warranty or recall times, the low end of what shops bill. Economy: Hyundai's 0.9 M/H is printed on the dealer notification for the bulletin; in the bulletin table it is on the Sonata row. Midsize: Hyundai's 0.5 MH is for the 2007-2008 Santa Fe itself. Truck: Toyota's 0.9 hrs/vehicle covers the 2009-2010 Tacoma itself and includes 0.1 hr of paperwork. Luxury: Lexus's 1.2 flat rate hours is for the 2023-2024 NX itself, includes 0.1 hr of paperwork, and may include a serial-number inspection. The only high figure is a signed DIY guide's 'about 2 hours' for the Elantra; it is used for economy and, as a not-this-vehicle figure, for midsize. Economy and truck prices use different part numbers, and truck and luxury rest on different bulletins and different parts.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis or code-scan fee, a steering angle sensor recalibration or reset where the car needs one, a new steering wheel bolt on vehicles where it is single-use, a steering angle sensor where it is sold as part of the clock spring or has to be replaced with it, shop supplies and sales tax. The driver airbag module and steering wheel switches are separate parts and are quoted separately if they are also needed.
